newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Tariff revision reports hit Pakistan energy sector.
newsitem.headline: Tariff revision reports hit Pakistan energy sector.

text.p: Pakistan's blue chip energy stocks tumbled on Thursday on reports of government plans to revise tariffs for buying electricity from private companies, but some analysts said the market over-reacted to the news.

"Any cuts in tariffs is impossible because of the guarantees given by the government in agreements with private power companies including Hub Power," said Ather Raouf, director of sales at WI Carr Mashriq.
The Hub Power Company Ltd tumbled 1.75 rupees to 37.75 at the provisional close of the Karachi Stock Exchange (KSE) on turnover of 16.4 million shares.
"There are no chances that the government can revise its power purchase tariffs with the companies already in production. But for the new entrants, it can apply its plans," Raouf said.

Local newspapers quoted Water and Power Minister Nisar Ali as saying on Wednesday that Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government would re-negotiate tariff agreements with the sponsors of private sector thermal power projects as the electricity purchase rates were too high.
"We cannot pass on this electricity to the consumers at such high prices," the daily Business Recorder quoted Ali as saying. "The price of 6.5 cents per unit is not acceptable to us."
Ali's remarks triggered sale energy stocks and weakened overall sentiment at the KSE, dealers said.
"The news jolted the market because the earnings of private power projects will come down if agreements are re-negotiated," dealer Shakil Anwar said.
"Investors are jittery and lack confidence regarding consistency in government policies."
Anwar said the entire energy sector had been hit by the news and analysts saw sharp falls in the earnings of private power companies if the government went ahead with such a plan.
But Baring Securities, in its daily review, said the minister had not outlined any specifics of such re-negotiations.

"There is a possibility that the companies might be asked to look at their cost structures carefully to review each element and make adjustments where there is room to do so," said Aliya Ehmar of ING Baring Securities.
Hina Akhlaq of KASB & Co said a revision of power tariffs was possible as state-run power companies were faced with acute financial problems.

To bail out financially strapped state-run Water and Power Development Authority (WAPDA) and the Karachi Electricity Supply Corporation, the government had little choice but to increase power charges and cut tariff rates of private companies, she said.

But dealers said the World Bank, which has an equity or debt stake in power projects such as Hub Power, would oppose any cut in tariff rates and would also like to be reassured about its debt repayment by the WAPDA by increased electricity prices.
